Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
737 PM EDT Sun Aug 23 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 730 PM EDT Sunday...

Thunderstorm activity has begun to weaken. A rumble or two may
take place in the Champlain Valley, but the severe threat is
over for the evening. Quiet conditions are expected tonight.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 250 PM EDT Sunday...

1. Numerous showers and embedded thunderstorms will continue 
across the region this afternoon, with some isolated strong to 
severe thunderstorms possible.  

2. Lingering showers will continue into the start of the week 
under broad cyclonic flow, with drier weather returning towards the 
middle of the week. 

3. Showers with some thunderstorm potential to end the week 
will be followed by another tranquil period over the weekend.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 250 PM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Gusty showers continue to bubble up across the region 
this afternoon as a frontal boundary continues to move through the 
region. Some more embedded thunderstorms are expected to develop as 
the afternoon progresses, especially with clearing skies allowing 
for more instability over the next few hours. CAPE values are 
expected to reach around 1000-1500 J/kg this afternoon, which will 
help with the thunderstorm development, along with modest lapse 
rates and shear. SPC continues to show the entire forecast area in a 
Marginal Risk for severe weather this afternoon with the idea that a 
few isolated strong to severe thunderstorms are possible, with 
possible hail and strong winds as the primary threats. Storms looks 
to be progressive, limiting any hydro concerns at this time, 
especially given the dry weather the last few days. The current 
forecast still shows about 0.20 to 0.50 inches across much of the 
area, with lower totals expected across much of the Northeast 
Kingdom and some higher amounts possible within any thunderstorms 
that develop. Shower activity will gradually wane through this 
evening as the frontal boundary exits the region, although some 
showers may linger overnight, especially across northern New York. 
Some clearing may be possible tonight behind the system, which may 
lead to some fog/mist developing overnight, especially in locations 
that see rainfall today as there will be plenty of moisture, 
although winds may be enough to limit this potential. Overnight lows 
are expected to generally be in the upper 40s and 50s tonight, with 
temperatures near Lake Champlain near 60.

KEY MESSAGE 2: For the start of the week, the region will remain in 
broad cyclonic flow, will will allow for linger showers on Monday 
and Tuesday, especially across the higher terrain as the upper level 
low gradually shifts away from the region. This cyclonic flow will 
also lead to some lake effect showers off Lake Ontario, with 
increased shower chances expected across northern New York Monday 
into Tuesday. Temperatures will be on the cool side, with highs only 
climbing into the 70s, with some locations in the Adirondacks 
struggling to climb out of the upper 60s. A brief period of ridging 
looks to build into the region for Wednesday, bringing some drier 
weather conditions for the middle of the week.

KEY MESSAGE 3: A broad upper-level trough remains on track to progress 
into the eastern Great Lakes by Thursday afternoon, putting us in a 
favorable position for showers and thunderstorms. The probability of 
thunderstorms compared to 24 hours ago has trended quite a bit 
higher for this timeframe, with the latest NBM 6 hour thunder 
chances (2 PM to 8 PM) now in the 25 to 32% range across our region. 
Relatedly, forecast temperatures have ticked up with highs favored 
to reach the upper 70s to mid 80s amidst seasonably humid conditions 
with dewpoints in the low to mid 60s during peak heating. Generally 
the potential for stronger storms is low but appears to be slightly 
elevated in northern New York relative to Vermont where both CAPE 
and shear will likely be somewhat higher.

With a surface low and associated trough slow to push eastward, 
shower chances will continue through Thursday night into Friday 
morning, which makes the convective chances for Friday questionable. 
However, signals for higher instability relative to Thursday, 
especially in Vermont, still exists in many pieces of ensemble 
guidance. The large scale pattern with continued height falls and 
cold front still to our west suggests scattered showers and 
thunderstorms are a good bet for Friday afternoon, especially if 
there is enough surface heating. Given convective nature of a lot of 
the rain, rainfall amounts will likely be highly variable, but 
overall the potential for excessive rain is minimal at this time 
without particularly rich moisture. 48 hour probabilities of 
rainfall exceeding an inch per latest NBM are only as high as 22% 
and mainly under 10% in our region. 

As the system's low pressure area occludes near Hudson Bay, a ridge 
of high pressure will build in to the south and expand across the 
northeastern US by Saturday morning, providing us with low humidity 
and seasonable conditions for the weekend. Perhaps by the end of the 
weekend the gyre will be forced southward and precipitation chances 
increase, but the predictability of such a scenario is low at this 
time.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Through 00Z Tuesday...Two strips of precipitation are crossing
the Vermont-New Hampshire border and in the Champlain Valley.
Portions of Vermont may see some showers for a couple more
hours, but mostly quiet conditions are expected. There are mixed
signals for fog tonight. Under the influence of cooler low 
pressure to our west, lake effect activity will stream into
northern New York. This should bring some clouds over KSLK with
ceilings around 2000-3000 ft agl, but KMPV and KRUT are the 
most likely to experience fog tonight, but there will be some 
light winds possible overnight and so 3SM is shown given the
uncertainty. South to southeast winds are expected to trend 
towards 5 knots, and then after 14z, increase to 7 to 12 knots 
sustained with gusts 16 to 22 knots possible. Additional shower 
activity is likely Monday afternoon, first over KSLK about 
15z-21z, and then 18z-23z for most others. Precipitation will be
scattered, and so mainly PROB30s were used.

Outlook...

Monday Night: VFR. Chance SHRA.
Tuesday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Chance SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.
Tuesday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. NO SIG WX.

Wednesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.

Thursday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Likely
SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Friday: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA, Slight
chance TSRA.
